While the machine still operates with modest qubit counts compared with larger road‑maps, its presence will accelerate local expertise and could spur region‑specific applications ranging from materials science to finance.

item.title: Oracle Launches Java 27 Featuring Hybrid Post-Quantum Cryptography for TLS 1.3
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article is noteworthy because it marks one of the first mainstream programming platform releases that embeds hybrid post‑quantum key exchange directly into TLS 1.3, signaling a shift from experimental libraries to production‑grade software ready for enterprise deployment. By pairing NIST‑standardized algorithms in Oracle Jipher 20 with classic curves, the update gives developers an immediate path to quantum‑resilient communications without rewriting existing codebases. It also underscores how the broader industry is moving from “prepare‑later” post‑quantum roadmaps toward concrete, interoperable solutions as quantum hardware edges closer to breaking current cryptography. Readers should note that hybrid schemes still rely on classical primitives for security, so full protection will only materialize once pure post‑quantum suites are widely vetted and standardized.

Oracle has released Java 27 (Oracle JDK 27), introducing significant security and performance updates. A key feature is the integration of hybrid post-quantum cryptography for TLS 1.3, designed to protect against future quantum decryption threats. This release also includes Oracle Jipher 20 for NIST-standardized quantum-resistant algorithms and various performance optimizations. item.title: QuTech Spinout Q*Bird Rebrands to Falqon Systems to Commercialize Quantum Secure Networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks a key step toward the commercialization of quantum‑grade cybersecurity, as Falqon Systems moves from prototype hardware to full‑stack Quantum Secure Networks that can protect real‑world data traffic. By leveraging measurement‑device‑independent QKD, the company sidesteps many practical vulnerabilities that have slowed earlier field trials and aligns its rollout with the EuroQCI roadmap, accelerating Europe’s push for a continent‑wide quantum communication backbone. If Falqon can deliver scalable, interoperable services across borders, it could set the de‑facto standard for quantum‑safe links in finance, government and critical infrastructure—though widespread adoption will still hinge on cost reductions and integration with existing telecom ecosystems.

Q*Bird has rebranded to Falqon Systems, signaling its expansion from hardware manufacturing to deploying end-to-end Quantum Secure Networks (QSN). The company, a spinout from QuTech and TU Delft, will continue with its existing leadership and technological roadmaps, focusing on its integrated platform built upon Measurement-Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (MDI-QKD) for enhanced security and scalability in quantum communication. Falqon Systems currently operates across several European countries, aligning with the European Quantum Communication Infrastructure (EuroQCI) initiative. item.description:
Curator's Take: This article highlights a rare transatlantic partnership that injects $10 million into molecular quantum information science, a niche where chemistry meets qubit engineering and could unlock scalable spin‑based processors. By funding eight teams to design custom molecules and model quantum state transfer, the program builds on recent advances in molecular spin qubits from both the US and UK, accelerating the move from proof‑of‑concept devices toward chemically tailored hardware. The investment signals growing policy support for bottom‑up quantum architectures, but readers should note that practical quantum computers based on these molecules are still years away as synthesis challenges and coherence times remain open questions.

The NSF and UKRI have jointly committed $10 million to fund eight transatlantic research teams in molecular quantum information science. This initiative, with $5 million from NSF and £3.7 million from UKRI, focuses on foundational chemistry research to manipulate quantum states in complex molecular architectures. This second phase of funding aims to synthesize custom molecular systems, engineer molecular-scale spin qubits, and model quantum information transfer, directly supporting international research partnerships. item.description:

By demonstrating that metallic plasmonic resonances can be harnessed without the heating and loss problems that have plagued superconducting and ion‑trap systems, the work could bridge the long‑standing stability‑versus‑scalability trade‑off that has limited every other platform. If the approach scales as promised, it would give hardware developers a material‑based shortcut to denser quantum processors, but the results still hinge on reproducible nanofabrication and low‑temperature performance that remain to be proven in full‑scale chips.

How two research teams and a London based quantum hardware company are betting nanoscale gold can crack the stability-scalability problem that has stalled every other qubit platform. It builds on the momentum of the EU Quantum Flagship and recent national chip‑program investments, positioning CSIC’s QuARC network alongside other emerging foundries in the US and Asia to accelerate hardware convergence across computing, sensing and cryptography. While the facility promises faster iteration cycles for research groups and industry partners, scaling those prototypes into manufacturable volumes will still require broader ecosystem support and supply‑chain coordination.

Spain's CSIC has opened a Quantum Nanofabrication Area at IMB-CNM in Barcelona, a €6 million investment funded by Spain's PERTE Chip program and NextGenerationEU. This facility, equipped with advanced lithography and microscopy systems, is designed for prototyping quantum hardware like QPUs and QKD components. item.title: IonQ, ORNL, NVIDIA, and UT Knoxville Advance AI-Driven Generative Quantum Circuit Synthesis
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases a genuine leap in quantum‑software engineering by using a transformer‑based AI model—DQAOA‑GPT—to generate high‑quality QAOA circuits without the costly trial‑and‑error tuning that has long bottlenecked hybrid optimization workflows. By slashing synthesis time to a fixed 28 seconds and delivering roughly twice the solution fidelity on higher‑order unconstrained binary problems, the work builds directly on recent pushes toward AI‑assisted quantum compilation from both academia and industry. If the approach scales to larger qubit counts, it could dramatically accelerate the deployment of near‑term variational algorithms on hardware such as IonQ’s trapped‑ion processors. Nonetheless, performance gains remain demonstrated only on benchmark HUBO instances, so broader validation across diverse problem families will be essential before the method becomes a standard tool in quantum algorithm pipelines.

A collaboration between ORNL, IonQ, NVIDIA, and UT Knoxville introduced DQAOA-GPT, a generative AI framework that synthesizes quantum optimization circuits, eliminating iterative parameter-tuning. This framework significantly reduces circuit synthesis runtime to a constant 28 seconds and doubles solution quality for higher-order unconstrained binary optimization (HUBO) problems, as presented at IEEE Quantum Week 2026. DQAOA-GPT replaces traditional trial-and-error with a transformer model trained on high-performing circuit profiles, allowing hybrid algorithms to scale subproblem sizes efficiently. item.title: Oxford Quantum Circuits and Trust Base Benchmark Hybrid Quantum Workloads for Financial Risk Modeling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article is noteworthy because it provides one of the first systematic comparisons of purely classical, hybrid quantum‑classical and fully fault‑tolerant approaches on a real‑world finance problem, showing where quantum methods currently excel (parameter efficiency in QPINNs) and where they still lag (runtime stability). By highlighting how Quantum Signal Processing could shrink Quantum Monte Carlo resource needs and how tighter error‑correction thresholds would dramatically lower the qubit count for fault‑tolerant implementations, the work connects directly to ongoing hardware roadmaps from OQC and broader industry pushes toward practical quantum advantage. Readers should care because it maps a realistic pathway—from near‑term hybrid algorithms to future fault‑tolerant processors—for financial institutions that are already exploring quantum risk analytics, while also reminding them that substantial engineering challenges remain before those gains can be realized.

Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) and Trust Base benchmarked hybrid quantum workloads for financial risk modeling, evaluating classical, hybrid quantum-classical, and fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for tasks like derivative pricing and Value-at-Risk. The study found that while Quantum-compressed Physics-Informed Neural Networks (QPINNs) showed parameter efficiency, classical PINNs offered better runtimes and stability. Optimizations like Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) could significantly reduce resource requirements for Quantum Monte Carlo, and improved hardware error correction thresholds could drastically cut the physical qubit footprint for fault-tolerant quantum computing. item.title: Quobly Demonstrates Single-Chip Readout and Gates on 300mm Industrial Silicon Process
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first time a full qubit control stack—readout, single‑qubit rotations and two‑qubit entangling gates—has been demonstrated on a 300 mm industrial silicon wafer, proving that quantum circuits can be fabricated alongside classical CMOS in a standard foundry flow. By showing that the QSOI® architecture works at scale, Quobly bridges the gap between laboratory‑grade devices and mass‑manufacturable hardware, a step that aligns with recent moves by IBM, Intel and Google toward silicon‑based qubits. The announced cloud access to the Alloy Pioneer system and an ambitious million‑qubit target illustrate how quickly commercial timelines are tightening, though achieving error rates low enough for fault tolerance on such large chips remains a major hurdle.

Quobly has successfully demonstrated single-chip execution of qubit readout, single-qubit gates, and two-qubit gates on its QSOI® architecture, fabricated on an industrial 300mm silicon process at STMicroelectronics. This achievement validates their technology transfer strategy, allowing co-integration of quantum and classical circuitry. With plans for cloud access to their Alloy Pioneer system by late 2026 and a long-term target of one million qubits by 2032, Quobly is advancing its commercial and scaling roadmap, supported by significant Series A funding and strategic partnerships. By providing an open, pure‑play foundry, the effort directly tackles the current bottleneck in QPU scaling that has forced many startups to rely on limited university or legacy CMOS facilities, and it dovetails with recent government pushes to secure a domestic microelectronics supply chain for quantum technologies. The move also signals that the industry is maturing beyond prototype labs toward an ecosystem where multiple vendors can access standardized, high‑yield quantum chips, although achieving commercial yields at this scale will still require significant process refinement.

Anderon LLC, an IBM subsidiary, secured $1 billion in CHIPS Act funding, supplemented by another $1 billion from IBM, to expand its 300mm pure-play quantum wafer fabrication facility at Albany NanoTech. This investment aims to scale production of superconducting qubit arrays and other quantum components, addressing QPU scaling bottlenecks and strengthening domestic microelectronics supply chains. The facility will serve as an open commercial foundry for the global quantum hardware ecosystem. item.title: Continuous variable distributed quantum sensing in integrated photonics
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first demonstration of continuous‑variable entanglement‑enhanced sensing on a fully integrated photonic chip, showing that four distributed phase parameters can be measured with a precision modestly below the shot‑noise limit. By moving from bulk‑optic setups to an on‑chip architecture, it proves that scalable quantum sensor networks are feasible using deterministic squeezed‑light sources and on‑chip homodyne detection—a key step toward practical quantum‑enhanced metrology in compact devices. While the 0.2 dB gain is still small, the work establishes a platform that can be expanded to larger arrays and more complex sensing tasks as integrated photonics matures.

Distributed quantum sensing is an emerging application of quantum networking, where entangled probe states are employed to sense combinations of delocalized parameters with enhanced precision relative to using separable states. Squeezed states of light are a prime resource for experimental demonstrations of entanglement-enhanced sensing, because they can be generated and entangled deterministically. Existing distributed quantum sensing experiments have been fundamentally limited in scalability due to their bulk-optic architectures. Meanwhile, integrated photonics provides a scalable and compact platform for quantum sensors. Here we demonstrate entanglement-enhanced sensing of linear functions of four phase shifts in an integrated photonic circuit. We find an entanglement-enhanced precision of 0.199(16) dB below the shot noise limit compared to 0.041(18) dB for separable states. A four-mode entangled state is generated on-chip with entanglement verification and phase sensing also performed on-chip with an array of four integrated homodyne detectors.

item.title: Logarithmic-depth quantum simulation of boson sampling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the notoriously hard‑to‑simulate boson‑sampling problem can be reproduced by a logarithmic‑depth qubit circuit built from standard Clifford + T gates, meaning the task sits inside shallow quantum computation rather than requiring deep, fault‑tolerant architectures. By expanding the optical network into six quadratic shears and spreading each mode over many submodes, the authors achieve a fixed local occupation cutoff that enables parallel phase operations and a single final measurement—an approach that dovetails with recent pushes for low‑depth algorithms on near‑term devices. The result suggests boson sampling may be experimentally accessible sooner than expected, though it still demands polynomially many qubits and careful error control to reach the inverse‑polynomial total‑variation accuracy claimed.

We show that boson sampling with an arbitrary $m$-mode interferometer and $n\le m$ single-photon inputs can be simulated to inverse-polynomial total-variation error by a logarithmic-depth qubit circuit with polynomially many qubits. The circuit uses Clifford+$T$ gates, arbitrary qubit connectivity, and a single final measurement, and its family is logspace uniform. The key idea is to enlarge the optical system, decompose the resulting transformation into six quadratic shears, and distribute each mode over many submodes. This redistribution permits a fixed local occupation cutoff, after which local basis changes and parallel phase gates give the qubit circuit. Consequently, our result places boson sampling within shallow quantum computation.

item.title: Entanglement swapping across a five-node relay in a multiplexed quantum-classical network
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first time entanglement swapping has been achieved across a five‑node relay while sharing the same C‑band fibers with live 10‑Gbps classical traffic, demonstrating that quantum repeaters can coexist with today’s telecom infrastructure. By quantifying the fidelity‑Raman‑noise trade‑off and showing successful swapping over four × 10 km spans, the work provides a concrete roadmap for integrating quantum links into existing backbone networks rather than requiring dedicated dark fibers. The result brings practical, large‑scale quantum networking—and its promised secure communication and distributed sensing capabilities—closer to real‑world deployment.

Quantum networks are resources for scaling quantum computers and distributed sensing technologies while offering post-quantum security benefits. Teleporting non-classical resources like entanglement, via so called entanglement swapping, is essential for networks in particular overcoming rate-loss limits via quantum repeaters. Deploying these systems on real infrastructure will likely require multiplexing photonic qubits into fibers carrying 'classical' light encoding standard Internet communications and control plane signals for multi-node quantum protocols. Here, we report the first demonstration of entanglement swapping and conventional communications operating over the same fibers. Entanglement is swapped across a five-node quantum relay topology connected by four long-distance fibers, each populated with classical data signals. Time-bin entangled photons in the C-band are multiplexed alongside C-band classical signals using dense-wavelength division multiplexing, introducing noise photons generated by high-power classical light. We experimentally and theoretically characterize the trade-off between quantum fidelity and Raman noise photons. Entanglement swapping is demonstrated over a maximum fiber length of 40 km (four 10-km fibers) while simultaneously transmitting 10-Gbps classical data through all fibers. These results represent a significant advancement in the demonstrated complexity of coexisting quantum and classical networks and provide a roadmap for achieving the widespread deployment of advanced quantum technologies.

item.title: Feasibility Ordering of Entanglement-Source Placement for Qubit Channels
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a standing conjecture by proving that, for any pair of noisy qubit channels, placing an entanglement source at the midpoint can never be worse than putting it at an endpoint—a result that holds in the strict feasibility sense used to define “optimal” placement. By linking the sequential composition of channels to their parallel action through a novel transpose‑factorization argument and quantum Sinkhorn scaling, the work provides a rigorous foundation for designing quantum repeaters and satellite links without having to fine‑tune source locations for each hardware configuration. The finding streamlines network planning for near‑term quantum communication systems, though it addresses only the binary question of whether entanglement can survive, not the quantitative rates or fidelities that ultimately determine practical performance.

This work studies the placement of an entanglement source along a communication line formed by two noisy qubit channels. Recent work argued, on analytical and numerical grounds, that midpoint placement should be at least as favorable as endpoint placement. Here it is shown that, for arbitrary qubit channels, if a sequential composition can preserve entanglement, then the corresponding parallel action cannot annihilate all entanglement. The proof uses the transpose-factorization criterion introduced in that recent work. Quantum Sinkhorn scaling converts every strictly positive qubit channel into a unital representative, and the special normal form of unital qubit channels then yields the required factorization of the transposed map through the original channel. Depolarizing regularization and the closedness of the set of entanglement-breaking channels extend the result to arbitrary channels. Consequently, $Λ_1 \otimes Λ_2 \in \mathrm{EA}$ implies $Λ_2 \circ Λ_1 \in \mathrm{EB}$, and, by exchanging the two channels, the same holds for the opposite composition order. This proves the recent conjecture that midpoint placement is optimal for all qubit channels, in the feasibility sense in which that optimality was originally defined.

item.title: Query-Optimal and Gate-Efficient Lindbladian Simulation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers a Lindbladian‑simulation algorithm whose query complexity meets the known lower bound for Hamiltonian simulation, showing that open‑system dynamics can be simulated with essentially no extra overhead beyond closed‑system evolution. By leveraging block‑encoded Hamiltonians and a compact Kraus‑label representation, it extends recent advances in quantum signal processing and compressed sensing to dissipative processes, positioning it as a natural next step after the wave of optimal Hamiltonian‑simulation results. The approach promises more efficient modeling of noise, decoherence, and non‑unitary chemistry on fault‑tolerant hardware, though its practical impact will depend on how readily the required block and projected‑unitary oracles can be constructed for real devices.

We give a quantum algorithm for Lindbladian simulation given a block encoding of the Hamiltonian $H$ and a projected unitary encoding of the stacked jump operator $B=\sum_{k=1}^m \lvert k\rangle\otimes L_k$, with normalization factors $α_H$ and $α_B$, respectively. For evolution time $t$, set $τ=(α_H+α_B^2)t$. The algorithm approximates the evolution channel to diamond-norm error $\varepsilon$ using $O\!\left(τ+\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log\!\left(e+\log(1/\varepsilon)/τ\right)}\right)$ oracle queries, matching the query lower bound for Hamiltonian simulation. The number of additional one- and two-qubit gates is linear in the query complexity up to polylogarithmic factors. The query- and gate-complexity bounds extend to Lipschitz-continuous time-dependent Lindbladians under coherent time-indexed oracle access. Our construction uses a one-query transducer that implements a product of rational approximations to short-time evolution when supplied with a catalyst. We bound the error from omitting the catalyst by exploiting orthogonality between different sequences of Kraus labels. The gate implementation combines a compressed Kraus-label representation, which stores only the positions and values of the nonzero labels, with the rotation factorization of Chen et al.

item.title: Theory-agnostic nonclassicality certification in an integrated photonic circuit
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first theory‑independent verification of generalized contextuality on a three‑mode silicon photonic chip, showing that nonclassical behavior can be certified without presuming any specific quantum model. By marrying theory‑agnostic tomography with simplex‑embeddability tests, the work bridges foundational physics and the scalable hardware platform that underpins most near‑term photonic quantum processors. The result bolsters confidence in device‑independent protocols for future photonic quantum advantage, while highlighting that rigorous certification still demands careful experimental control to rule out classical embeddings.

Certifying nonclassicality without assuming any particular underlying physical theory constitutes both a foundational challenge and a requirement for device-independent protocols. Realizing such theory-independent certification in scalable architectures is essential for connecting fundamental tests with emerging quantum technologies. Integrated photonic circuits are a leading platform for scalable quantum information processing, motivating the development of rigorous methods to certify the nonclassical resources underpinning quantum advantage. In this paper, we report a theory-independent certification of generalized contextuality on a three-mode integrated photonic circuit. Our approach combines theory-agnostic tomography with simplex-embeddability certification---a framework that requires no assumptions about the underlying physical theory---and applies it to experimental data from a three-mode photonic circuit seeded by single photons. An independently constructed quantum model of the experiment provides a consistency check on the observed nonclassicality, without entering the certification as a theoretical assumption. The method rules out simplex-embeddability for our experimental data, providing robust, theory-independent evidence that our photonic circuit exhibits nonclassicality.

item.title: Impact of a CSS quantum error correction code in underwater quantum key distribution
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that modest‑size CSS error‑correction codes can rescue vertical underwater BB84 QKD in the marginal signal‑to‑noise regimes where photon loss and solar background would otherwise abort key generation, delivering up to a 4.5 dB SNR advantage. By coupling a realistic stochastic model of Jerlov Type III water with analytical QBER and secure‑key‑rate calculations, it pinpoints depth‑range windows where the encoding overhead is outweighed by the extra robustness—information that could guide the design of quantum‑secure maritime sensor networks. The work also clarifies that at higher SNRs raw BB84 remains optimal, underscoring that QECC deployment must be carefully matched to channel conditions rather than applied universally.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables secure underwater communications essential for maritime infrastructure. Underwater optical channels introduce substantial photon loss (erasures) and ambient noise that degrade QKD performance. This paper investigates whether two four-qubit Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum error correction codes (QECC) mitigate these impairments in vertical underwater communication BB84 QKD protocol. After developing a comprehensive stochastic channel model incorporating photon loss, geometric spreading, and solar noise, we assess the viability of QECC through the analytical study of the quantum bit error rate (QBER) and the secure key rate (SKR) with and without security depending on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) validated against Monte Carlo simulations. The standard four-qubit CSS code achieves a 3 dB SNR gain at the QBER 11% security threshold; the discard code variant achieves 4.5 dB. However, QECC includes an encoding overhead that reduces the SKR. We demonstrate a crucial relationship between the SKR and the probability of arrival of the sent photon. Analysis shows that QECC is beneficial exclusively in marginal SNR regimes; at high SNR, raw BB84 dominates. For an ocean Type III Jerlov water scenario with sunlight coming from the sun located at the top of the atmosphere, we identify operational depth-range windows where QECC enables communication otherwise infeasible. This analysis establishes that error correction deployment must be scenario-dependent: extend operational range at the cost of throughput when SNR is marginal, or prioritize key generation rates at high SNR.

item.title: Learning to Program Adaptive Non-Local Observables for Machine Learning
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that quantum neural networks can break free of the long‑standing bottleneck of local measurements by using a hypernetwork to program both circuit parameters and multi‑qubit observables on a per‑input basis, a capability previously limited to static observables. By achieving state‑of‑the‑art mean‑squared error on several multivariate time‑series benchmarks and consistently outperforming ANO‑based baselines in reinforcement‑learning tasks, the work shows that adaptive non‑local observables can translate into tangible performance gains for practical machine‑learning workloads. While the results are currently validated on simulators, they point toward a new class of hardware‑aware QNN architectures that could leverage emerging multi‑qubit readout technologies to deliver quantum advantage in data‑driven applications.

Quantum neural networks (QNNs) are typically built from variational quantum circuits (VQCs), which are limited by local measurements. Adaptive non-local observables (ANO) address this by jointly optimizing circuit parameters and multi-qubit measurements. However, existing ANO-based VQCs learn only a single static observable that remains invariant across all inputs. We propose QFWP-ANO, a novel architecture which employs a classical hypernetwork to dynamically program VQC parameters and/or non-local observables conditioned on each input. On multivariate time-series forecasting across four ETT datasets, QFWP-ANO achieves the lowest MSE in 16 of 20 settings and second-lowest in the remaining four, surpassing ANO-based and other strong baselines. On reinforcement learning tasks, QFWP-ANO consistently surpasses ANO-VQCs. Our results establish input-conditioned ANO as an effective approach for enhancing QNNs.

item.title: Variational Quantum Transformer Architecture for Synthetic Language Generation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it delivers the first concrete, NISQ‑compatible transformer‑style architecture for quantum natural‑language processing, showing that autoregressive token generation can be mapped onto variational quantum circuits with a realistic four‑token vocabulary. By benchmarking several variants against a compact classical transformer, the work situates QNLP within the broader push to embed deep‑learning primitives into near‑term hardware and highlights both the promise of learnable grammar structures and the practical hurdles such as initialization sensitivity. Readers should care that the study provides a tangible blueprint for hybrid quantum‑classical sequence models, offering a stepping stone toward more ambitious language tasks once larger, less noisy devices become available.

We propose a compact NISQ-compatible quantum transformer architecture for synthetic QNLP sequence modelling. The model preserves the autoregressive next-token interface of a classical transformer, but replaces attention and feed-forward sublayers with variational quantum encoder blocks, connector circuits, decoder blocks and a direct two-qubit measurement readout. Token contexts are angle-encoded into small quantum registers, processed by parallel variational heads and encoder integration circuits and conditioned through decoder ancillae to produce a distribution over a four-token vocabulary. We evaluate several architecture variants on deterministic and lexicographic grammar-generation tasks against a compact classical transformer baseline. The quantum models are trainable end-to-end and learn nontrivial grammar structure, including perfect deterministic generation in individual runs and high lexicographic validity in the strongest variant. The classical baseline remains more accurate and stable and the quantum models are sensitive to initialization. The contribution is therefore not a claim of quantum advantage, but a concrete architecture and evaluation of transformer-inspired QNLP sequence modelling under near-term quantum constraints.

item.title: Programmable Hong--Ou--Mandel interference in a giant-atom beam splitter
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a giant atom coupled to two waveguides can be tuned to act as a programmable Hong‑Ou‑Mandel interferometer, giving continuous control over single‑photon beam splitting and the resulting two‑photon bunching or antibunching statistics. By exploiting coupling‑phase differences, the device can switch between an effective 50:50 splitter and other asymmetric configurations without any hardware redesign, linking directly to recent advances in waveguide QED and reconfigurable photonic quantum processors. The authors also demonstrate that the same interference pattern can be used for high‑precision estimation of the atom’s coupling phases, suggesting a dual role as both a quantum logic element and a metrological sensor. Practical impact will hinge on achieving low‑loss, phase‑stable implementations in superconducting or integrated‑photonic platforms.

The Hong--Ou--Mandel (HOM) effect is a hallmark of two-photon quantum interference, in which two indistinguishable photons impinging on a balanced beam splitter bunch into the same output port. Here, we show that a giant atom (GA), coupled to two waveguides through two coupling points each, can function as a programmable HOM interferometer, enabling continuous control over single-photon beam splitting and two-photon interference. This programmability arises from coupling-phase differences in the GA, which tune its self-interference and directionality, and thereby its scattering response. To characterize the two-photon interference, we analyze the scattering of two Gaussian single-photon wave packets injected through different waveguides and evaluate the bunching and antibunching (coincidence) probabilities of the resulting four output ports. At the operating point where the GA acts as an effective 50:50 beam splitter for single photons, we observe a pronounced HOM dip as the relative input delay between the two wave packets is varied. Away from this point, adjusting the coupling phases continuously tunes the two-photon output statistics between bunching into the same output port and antibunching across distinct output ports. In addition, we explore an application to quantum parameter estimation, showing that small deviations of coupling phases can be estimated from the two-photon output statistics, with the achievable sensitivity quantified by the classical Fisher information associated with a binary coincidence measurement. Our giant-atom beam splitter thus provides a programmable platform for two-photon interference in waveguide quantum electrodynamics, with potential applications in quantum information processing, quantum communication, and quantum sensing.

item.title: Chiral classical and quantum acoustics with hole-spin qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates how surface‑acoustic waves can be harnessed to drive hole‑spin qubits with a tunable “spin‑acoustic chirality,” turning the direction of a phonon into a controllable knob for either spin rotations or frequency shifts. By linking a multiband Luttinger‑Kohn model to realistic piezoelectric finite‑element simulations, the authors quantify both the classical driving strength and the single‑phonon coupling, revealing an anisotropic Rabi interaction that enables directional one‑phonon emission—a capability that could simplify wiring and improve connectivity in large‑scale quantum processors. The work builds on recent advances in strain‑mediated qubit control and suggests practical routes to phonon‑based error protection and heralded entanglement, though experimental verification of the predicted chirality tuning will be essential before it can be integrated into hardware roadmaps.

Gate-defined hole spins combine strong spin-orbit coupling with exceptional strain sensitivity, making surface acoustic waves a natural route to remote, phase-coherent control. We show that counterpropagating surface acoustic waves can differ in coupling strength and in whether they predominantly drive spin rotations or modulate the qubit frequency. We call the transverse transition-strength imbalance spin-acoustic chirality and show that it is tunable through gate-controlled reshaping of the dot confinement. Combining a multiband Luttinger-Kohn Hamiltonian with the Bir-Pikus description of strain and 3D piezoelectric finite-element simulations, we obtain the acoustic g-matrix modulation governing coherent SAW driving. Quantizing the same strain-mediated interaction yields the corresponding single-phonon coupling, and a generalized anisotropic Rabi interaction with co-rotating, counter-rotating, and longitudinal components, linking classical chirality to quantum anisotropy and directional one-phonon emission. Magnetic field orientation and dot shape tune the acoustic chirality and operator selectivity. We illustrate this framework through bichromatic coherence protection and phonon-mediated heralded Bell-state initialization.

item.title: Optical Quantum Computing
item.description:

Under the label of optical quantum computing, there are a variety of protocols and experiments that use the quantum properties of light to achieve a computational advantage over classical computing machines. In this review, we describe some of the main implementations, which differ in the type of encoding and in how the computation is performed, whether using gates or cluster states. For each protocol, we describe advantages and challenges with an overview of the experimental results obtained, summarized in tables. Because of the great relevance achieved in this field, there is a section dedicated to non-universal quantum computation with photons, where boson sampling, variational quantum eigensolvers, and quantum machine learning applications are described. The aim is to give the reader the broadest overview of the applications where photons and their quantum properties play a key role in computation.

item.title: Growing Einstein-Rosen Bridge with Multi-partite Entanglement
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that genuine multipartite entanglement can keep growing even after all bipartite entropies have plateaued, providing a new diagnostic of the expanding Einstein‑Rosen bridge in holographic black holes. By introducing a “multi‑entropy” that continues to rise linearly with time, the authors extend the ER=EPR correspondence into a regime where ordinary entropy measures become blind, and they demonstrate that this behavior appears both in SYK‑type models and in random states. The result bridges quantum information theory and quantum gravity, suggesting that multipartite correlations may be the key resource underlying spacetime growth and could inform future studies of complexity and scrambling. It also cautions that relying solely on bipartite entropies can miss important structure, highlighting the need for richer entanglement diagnostics in both theoretical and experimental settings.

Can quantum entanglement continue to grow even after the entanglement entropies of subsystems have saturated? We address this question using genuine multi-entropy, which probes multi-partite entanglement structure beyond bipartite entanglement. In a two-sided BTZ black hole, this quantity grows linearly with time after every subsystem entropy of a fixed tripartition has saturated, extending the interval in which entanglement detects Einstein-Rosen bridge growth. The result refines the ER=EPR relation by identifying multi-partite structure invisible to ordinary entanglement entropies. Some spin-chain models and the spatially partitioned Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model exhibit distinct transients, while the late-time plateau values in holography, the SYK model, and Haar-random states share a universal behaviour.

item.title: Unbounded Holevo additivity gaps in finite dimensions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that even for modest‑size quantum channels the Holevo quantity can exhibit arbitrarily large superadditivity when two uses are combined, overturning the long‑standing intuition that additivity gaps should be bounded in finite dimensions. By constructing explicit families of mixed‑unitary channels with a linear gap in output qubits and only quadratic growth in input size, the work extends recent random‑matrix and free‑probability results into concrete, hardware‑relevant settings. The finding reshapes how we think about classical capacity limits for realistic devices, reminding engineers that multi‑use coding strategies may unlock far more information than single‑shot analyses suggest—though the constructions remain highly structured and not yet directly implementable.

We establish unbounded two-use Holevo additivity gaps in finite dimensions. For each sufficiently large fixed integer $K$ and all sufficiently large $n$, we construct channels $T_n$ with output dimension $K^n$, input dimension $\exp(Θ_K(n^2))$, and \[ χ(T_n^{\otimes2})-2χ(T_n) \ge n\left[\frac{\log_2K}{K}-2\log_2(1+9/K)\right]-O(1/n). \] The gap is linear in output qubits, with an explicit quadratic input-qubit cost and an explicit threshold on $n$. We also obtain channels whose single-use Holevo quantity tends to zero while their two-use Holevo information, and hence classical capacity, diverges. The channels arise from structured tensor products of the complementary mixed-unitary channels used in Collins's free-probabilistic proof. We establish minimum-output-entropy gaps by combining Collins--Youn's product-group Haagerup inequality with Bordenave--Collins's quantitative strong-convergence estimates

item.title: A Case Study on Noise Resilient Operator Selection in Adaptive Variational Quantum Algorithms
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a blind spot in the scalability of ADAPT‑VQE by showing that realistic noise can derail the crucial operator‑selection step as well as the parameter optimization, threatening convergence on today’s devices. By systematically testing coherent and incoherent channels on a linear H₃ molecule and then demonstrating that a judicious mix of dynamical decoupling, zero‑noise extrapolation and Pauli twirling restores reliable convergence, the work provides concrete guidance for running adaptive variational algorithms on noisy intermediate‑scale quantum hardware. The findings bridge a gap between theoretical algorithm design and practical implementation, suggesting that near‑term error‑mitigation stacks can make ADAPT‑VQE viable for more complex chemistry problems.

Hardware noise has been shown to significantly impact the accuracy of ADAPT-VQE, a ground state preparation algorithm. While previous work has studied the impact of noise on its parameter optimization step, its impact on the critical operator selection step remains comparatively unexplored. In this work, we examine the impact of a variety of noise channels on this step, using a linear H$_3$ molecule as a test case. We show that, despite the selection criterion's natural resilience to some noise, both coherent and incoherent noise can prevent convergence for sufficiently high noise rates. We employ quantum error mitigation techniques--dynamical decoupling, zero noise extrapolation, and Pauli twirling--and show that when combined appropriately, these techniques are capable of restoring a successful convergence profile. Our results highlight how error mitigation can improve the performance of ADAPT-VQE and enable convergence in the presence of hardware noise, offering valuable insights into the implementation of the algorithm on near-term quantum hardware.

item.title: Beyond Hardware: Adaptive Algorithmic Control by State-Proxy Equalization
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a clever re‑allocation of limited computational effort during a run can rival—or even eclipse—raw hardware upgrades, introducing Adaptive Algorithmic Control (A2C) as a new software lever for quantum advantage. By proving the State‑Proxy Equalization theorem and using the evolving quantum state itself to gauge “hardness,” A2C boosts low‑energy sampling on problems up to 156 qubits by anywhere from 22 % to orders of magnitude without deeper circuits or more shots. The work underscores that, especially in the NISQ era, algorithmic adaptivity can be as decisive as qubit quality, though its full impact will depend on scaling to larger devices and integrating with existing error‑mitigation stacks.

Recent advances in quantum computing have been driven primarily by improvements in hardware. Here we show that substantial gains can instead arise from how finite computational resources are allocated throughout a quantum computation. We introduce Adaptive Algorithmic Control (A2C), a software paradigm founded on a State-Proxy Equalization theorem, which proves that the optimal allocation for a state-derived proxy-error functional equalizes cumulative computational hardness rather than physical time. The required computational hardness is inferred directly from the evolving quantum state, avoiding explicit reconstruction of the exponentially large many-body spectrum. Across quantum optimization problems containing up to 156 qubits, combining exact simulations, large-scale supercomputer computations and IBM quantum hardware experiments, A2C improves the low-energy sampling probabilities by $22\%$ to over $100,000\%$ under matched circuit depths and measurement budgets. These results demonstrate that quantum computational performance depends not only on hardware capabilities, but also on how finite computational resources are organized, establishing adaptive algorithmic control as a complementary software pathway for advancing quantum computation.

item.title: Quantum Compiler Design for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article spotlights a crucial shift from generic circuit optimization to encoding‑aware compilation that can actually bridge algorithm design with fault‑tolerant hardware constraints. By weaving together recent advances such as surface‑code lattice surgery, emerging qLDPC code‑surgery techniques, and real‑time decoder integration, it shows how a full‑stack compiler could slash the qubit overhead needed for logical operations on superconducting, trapped‑ion, and neutral‑atom platforms. Readers should care because these compiler innovations are among the most promising levers to bring practical quantum advantage within reach, even though many of the proposed pipelines still await experimental validation.

Scalable quantum computation is expected to rely on fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC), in which quantum error correction (QEC) suppresses physical errors sufficiently to support reliable logical operations. This requires quantum compilation to move beyond general-purpose circuit optimization toward encoding-aware and protocol-structured compilation across the full stack of fault-tolerant quantum computers. Beyond circuit synthesis and hardware mapping, an FTQC compiler must lower algorithm-level operations into the logical gate set supported by the chosen code, coordinate encoded data and ancilla resources, realize logical operations together with repeated syndrome extraction under hardware constraints, and provide the resulting measurement stream to real-time decoding. This survey presents a full-stack view of compiler design for QEC-protected quantum computation. We organize existing work into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC compilation, physical-level QEC realization, and decoder runtime integration. At the logical level, we review surface-code lattice-surgery compilers, beyond-surface-code code-surgery frameworks including emerging qLDPC approaches, and compilation support for non-Clifford operations such as magic-state distillation and code switching. At the physical level, we survey hardware-aware QEC realization on superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms. We further examine decoder models, real-time decoding systems, and frame-management mechanisms that close the feedback loop during fault-tolerant execution. Finally, we identify open challenges in cross-layer optimization, qLDPC compilation, compiler-decoder co-design, runtime adaptivity, and the development of integrated and benchmarkable FTQC compilation stacks. An actively maintained paper list is available at: github.com/chenghongz/QEC-compiler-design.

item.title: Optimal Linear-Rate Conversion of Unknown Mixed Qubit States via SWAP Tests
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the purity of an unknown qubit can be scaled up or down at a provably optimal linear rate using only SWAP‑test measurements and maximally mixed ancillas, eliminating the need for complex two‑qubit gates. By linking the conversion rates to the eigenvalues of the right‑logarithmic‑derivative Fisher information matrix, it gives the first operational meaning to the full (including imaginary) RLD metric in a concrete hardware protocol. The result opens a practical pathway for on‑the‑fly state purification or dilution in quantum sensors and near‑term processors, where controlling mixedness with minimal circuitry is a key bottleneck.

By consuming multiple copies of an unknown qubit state, one can modify its purity while preserving the direction of its Bloch vector. We determine the maximum linear rate at which qubit states of different purities can be interconverted, allowing a nonzero error, quantified, for instance, by the trace distance, provided that it vanishes in the limit of infinitely many copies. Interestingly, the optimal conversion rate is determined by the two eigenvalues of the complex right-logarithmic-derivative (RLD) Fisher information matrix associated with $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ rotations of the qubit state. When the output qubits have higher purity, corresponding to concentration, the optimal rate is given by the ratio of the maximum eigenvalues of the input and output RLD matrices. In contrast, when the output qubits have lower purity, corresponding to dilution, the optimal rate is given by the ratio of their minimum eigenvalues. Remarkably, both concentration and dilution can be implemented using SWAP tests as the only nontrivial two-qubit measurement primitive, together with ancillary qubits initially prepared in maximally mixed states, without requiring any additional two-qubit gates. Our work thus provides a novel operational interpretation of the full complex RLD Fisher information matrix. Crucially, its antisymmetric, purely imaginary part encodes geometric information beyond the statistical distance between density operators and plays an essential role in determining the optimal state-conversion rates.

item.title: Forbidden Subspaces in Quantum State Smoothing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article resolves a long‑standing ambiguity about the quantum state that exists between preparation and post‑selection by showing that positivity uniquely selects an interval of admissible orderings whenever the forbidden subspace aligns with eigenvectors of a full‑rank filtered state. The authors further demonstrate that when this alignment fails, the system exhibits contextuality that can be experimentally probed on a single qubit, linking abstract smoothing theory to near‑term hardware tests. By connecting the structure of the smallest forbidden subspaces to topological classes (even‑dimensional Haldane versus odd‑dimensional trivial), the work provides a new lens for classifying measurement records and could inform error‑mitigation strategies that exploit post‑selection symmetry. Readers should care because it bridges foundational questions about quantum trajectories with concrete signatures accessible on current superconducting or trapped‑ion platforms.

A system between a preparation and a post-selection has had no agreed state since 1964. With positivity as the criterion, a post-selection admits an interval of orderings around the symmetric one exactly when the subspace it forbids is spanned by eigenvectors of a full-rank filtered state. Otherwise it certifies contextuality, testable on a qubit. The averaged filtered state carries the entanglement spectrum of the record, so the smallest forbidden subspaces a symmetry allows are even-dimensional in the Haldane class and odd in the trivial one. That parity is the record's topological class.

item.title: Geometric quantifier of the incompatibility of single-particle property attribution in indistinguishable boson systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a concrete geometric measure of how strongly the properties of individual bosons resist simultaneous attribution, linking the abstract notion of indistinguishable‑particle entanglement directly to the layout of Majorana stars on the Bloch sphere. By extending the construction from qubits to higher‑dimensional qudits, it offers a unified tool that can be applied to current photonic and cold‑atom hardware where identical bosons are the native carriers of quantum information. The result not only deepens our theoretical understanding of multipartite entanglement in symmetric systems but also provides a practical benchmark for assessing and optimizing entanglement generation on emerging bosonic quantum processors.

Entanglement in indistinguishable particle systems can be characterized by the impossibility of unambiguously attributing a complete set of physical properties to the individual constituent particles. In this work, we introduce a geometric quantifier of the incompatibility of such simultaneous property attribution for pure states of $N$ indistinguishable bosons. Using the Majorana stellar representation, any symmetric multi-qubit state can be expressed as the symmetrization of constituent single-particle states, allowing the associated single-particle properties to be directly linked with the corresponding Majorana stars. This establishes a direct connection between the geometry of the Majorana representation on the Bloch sphere and the entanglement criterion based on the attribution of single-particle properties in systems of identical two-level bosons. We then generalize this geometric approach to higher-dimensional bosons, extending the quantifier from qubits to qudits, while retaining a geometric interpretation of property-attribution incompatibility in terms of Fubini-Study angles.

item.title: Large-scale NMR simulation on a trapped-ion quantum computer
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a trapped‑ion processor can now tackle NMR simulations far beyond the few‑spin examples that have dominated earlier demonstrations, delivering a faithful 21‑spin spectrum for a chemically relevant molecule. By combining a hardware‑efficient Hamiltonian reduction with tailored error suppression, the work bridges the gap between proof‑of‑principle experiments and simulations that could actually replace or augment classical NMR calculations in research and industry. While noise mitigation remains crucial, the result signals that digital quantum simulators are approaching the scale needed for practical chemical spectroscopy.

Simulating nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra is a promising application of quantum simulation. Using Quantinuum's System Model H2, a trapped-ion quantum computer, we demonstrate an end-to-end, large-scale digital NMR simulation of a classically challenging benchmark molecule, 1,2-di-tert-butyl-diphosphane. We implement a hardware-efficient reduction of the nuclear-spin Hamiltonian, enabling Trotterized real-time evolution of an effective 21-spin model with tailored error suppression to reduce the effects of device noise. The reconstructed liquid-state proton NMR spectrum agrees with classical reference calculations and reproduces key spectroscopic features that previous quantum hardware demonstrations did not capture. Given the widespread use of NMR in chemical analysis and industrial research, these results advance digital quantum simulation of NMR spectra towards practical quantum utility.

item.title: Probabilistic Error Cancellation for Single-Mode Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates how probabilistic error cancellation can be layered on top of Gottesman‑Kitaev‑Preskill (GKP) error correction, providing a concrete quantitative analysis of the sampling overheads required for both square and hexagonal GKP lattices. By comparing Steane‑type and teleportation‑based decoding under realistic finite‑squeezing noise, it shows that mitigation can meaningfully boost logical gate fidelity even when full fault tolerance is not yet achievable—a key step toward practical continuous‑variable quantum processors. The results give experimentalists a clear benchmark for how much extra classical sampling is needed to trade off hardware imperfections against algorithmic performance in near‑term devices.

In order to solve practical problems on a quantum computer, it is necessary to use fault-tolerant quantum error correction schemes to overcome noise: the errors arising from imperfections in physical components. The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code aims at achieving this in a hardware efficient manner by encoding finite-dimensional logical subspaces in the Hilbert space of one or more continuous variable modes. In near term implementations, however, it is not feasible to eliminate errors entirely, so it is natural to also employ alternative error mitigation techniques together with error correction. In this work, we study a quantum error mitigation method known as probabilistic error cancellation in the context of the GKP code. We compare Steane-type and teleportation-based GKP error correction, and calculate the sampling overheads associated with the technique for square and hexagonal GKP codes. We employ the stabilizer subsystem decomposition for GKP codes to obtain an effective logical channel for noisy operations that is used to express the ideal one of a target logical unitary. We consider noise from finite squeezing on the data and the two ancilla modes, needed for error correction, and examine the relationship between the sampling overhead and the noise for different decoding methods. Our results are calculated for single- and two-qubit GKP Clifford gates and one round of error correction, and show the nontrivial combination of error correction and mitigation in continuous variable codes.

item.title: Constant sized support state distillation with qubit recycling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that magic‑state distillation can be carried out with a fixed number of logical qubits by recycling idle qubits, dramatically shrinking the space‑time volume needed for high‑fidelity non‑Clifford gates. By extending code‑doubling techniques to every level of the Clifford hierarchy, it recovers known efficient protocols and introduces ultra‑compact $111\to1$ T‑state distillation at distance 7, a clear step toward practical fault‑tolerant quantum processors where qubit resources are scarce. The result dovetails with recent efforts to lower overhead in surface‑code architectures, though the schemes still rely on sufficiently low physical error rates to achieve the promised distances.

In order to circumvent that no universal set of gates can be achieved on a given quantum error-correcting codes, additional gates can be performed through magic state injection. This however requires to have access to high fidelity magic state, which can be obtained by the distillation of low quality states to fewer higher quality ones. In this paper, we provide a family of distillation protocols able to produce diagonal states at every level of the Clifford hierarchy. This family is obtained recursively using code doubling techniques and leveraging qubit recycling, the fact that some idle qubits of the protocols can be measured and re-used. At a given level of the Clifford hierarchy, we show that the protocols we derive can be performed at arbitrary high distance on a fix number of logical qubits. This family recovers many known efficient protocols, and uncovers new ones, such as a $111 \to 1$ protocol for $|T\rangle$ state distillation at distance $7$, which are the most compact in term of volume. Finally, we discuss possible extension of this framework for distillation protocols producing more than one output state.
